newsitem.title: USA: Electric deregulation sparks "green" power demand.
newsitem.headline: Electric deregulation sparks "green" power demand.

text.p: Looming deregulation of the U.S. electric industry has sparked renewed interest in solar and wind power as competitive sources of electricity in the years ahead, industry executives say.

While Congress considers mandating use of renewable energy in a deregulated electric industry, power producers say demand is rising from environmentally concerned consumers willing to pay more for "green" power.

In the latest indication of this growing demand for renewables, as solar and wind energy are known in the industry, Central and South West Corp. last week signalled plans to add up to 75 megawatts of renewable power to its Texas electric grid.

The Dallas-based utility holding company this month also will seek Texas regulatory approval to set up a "green" pricing programme to underwrite additional renewable generation and market the power directly to retail customers.

"I think that there was a clear message from customers to include renewables as a part of the overall mix and that they felt so strongly about it that they were willing to pay more for it," utility spokesman Larry Jones said.

According to recent surveys, seven in 10 Americans believe global warming is a serious threat to the environment, and three in four said they would pay higher electric prices for non-polluting renewable energy.

The first test of consumers' willingness to pay the price for green power will come in California, where the massive retail electric market is set to open to competition beginning as early as January 1998.

"They'll have the right to choose what type of power they buy," said Robert Kelly, chairman of Houston-based Enron Renewable Energy Corp., a unit of Enron Corp., the leading worldwide natural gas and electricity company.

The Houston-based company controls between 30 and 50 percent of U.S. renewable energy generation through its January 1997 acquisition of Zond Corp., which operates 14 windfarms generating 268 megawatts of electricity, he said.
"The wind business is basically getting bigger and bigger in size," Kelly said, both in projected revenues and the size of a new generation of wind turbines coming on line.

In Lake Benton, Minn., Enron is installing new 30-ton turbines that stand on 50-meter towers with rotors longer than the wingspan of a commercial airliner. The company recently received a grant from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory to develop an even larger turbine, Kelly said.

With no fuel costs or emissions, wind and solar power hold natural advantages over traditional nuclear, coal and even natural gas-fired plants. But the up-front costs of building wind and solar farms, and a lack of reliability on windless or cloudy days, render renewables uneconomical without subsidies.

"As the technologies continue to improve and the cost of fossil fuels tends to rise, the cost of whether to add renewable resources or fossil fuel resources becomes more comparable from a price standpoint," Central and South West's Jones said.

That's not to say there won't be losers in the push to reduce emissions from electric power plants. In Congress, environmentalists have backed mandates that non-hydropowered renewable electricity account for at least 10 percent of total domestic generation.

But natural gas suppliers -- which also can boast of an environmentally friendly fuel source -- say they stand to lose $700 million a year in sales for every 1 percent of renewable power mandated by Congress.

Requiring the use of solar and wind power also would have an unintended consequence of keeping prices artificially higher by forcing companies to keep surplus plants on line to back up unreliable solar and wind farms, opponents say.
"This has got 'Made in Washington' stamped all over it," said Nick Bush, president of the Washington, D.C.-based Natural Gas Supply Association.
